title: Come Light Our Hearts
summary_theology: An Advent prayer of waiting that asks God to bring light into hearts that are still in the dark, holding longing and trust together rather than resolving them early.
practical_worship_leadership: Works as a sung response after an Advent reading, under or beside the candle lighting, or as a short prayer song at the start of a set. It is a waiting song, so keep it before the announcement carols rather than after them.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test, since no audio was analyzed for this page. Try it with one instrument and one voice first. Decide how many times the prayer repeats before you add anything, and agree a clear ending in rehearsal so the room is not left guessing whether to keep singing.
editorial_markdown:
## What "Come Light Our Hearts" means

The song is a short prayer for Advent. It asks God to bring light into hearts that are still waiting in the dark, and it stays in the asking rather than hurrying to the answer. The writer's own note on the Rain for Roots release describes it coming out of her church's Advent liturgy and a need for something the congregation could sing while they waited. That origin shows in the shape of the text. There is longing in it, and there is trust in it, and the song does not make the congregation choose between the two.

That is the useful thing about it for a planner. The song waits rather than announces, which gives you something to sing in the weeks before the carols.

## What this song offers your service

Place it as the response after an Advent scripture reading, as the music under or beside the candle lighting, or as the opening prayer of a set in the first two weeks of Advent. It can also return each week of the season as a repeated prayer, which is a planning option rather than a promise about how quickly a room will learn it.

Its limit is the same as its strength. It does not tell the nativity story or name the gospel in full, so consider placing it beside a song or reading that does. It fits the waiting weeks best; whether it still serves on Christmas Eve depends on how your church shapes that service.

## Scripture for preparation

These are preparation choices for the leader, not the writer's stated sources. Read Psalm 130:5-6, where the psalmist waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning, which gives you the posture of the song in two verses. Read Isaiah 9:2 for the people in darkness who see a great light, the promise the prayer is reaching toward. Luke 1:78-79, Zechariah's words about the sunrise visiting those who sit in darkness, makes a short reading before the first repetition and leads naturally into a candle.

## Choose the recording and key

Two recordings carry this composition. Sandra McCracken's own version is on God's Highway, released September 9, 2016, on her [Bandcamp page](https://sandramccracken.bandcamp.com/track/come-light-our-hearts). The earlier Rain for Roots recording on Waiting Songs, released November 10, 2015, credits Sandra McCracken and Skye Peterson as lead vocalists on its [track page](https://rainforroots.bandcamp.com/track/come-light-our-hearts). Same song, two settings; pick the one that sounds like your room.

Integrity's [song page](https://integrityworship.com/songs/come-light-our-hearts-sandra-mccracken/) lists the key of E, a 6/8 meter and a tempo marking of 58. The page does not say which note value that number counts, so treat it as the publisher's marking rather than a click setting to copy. Those values belong to the publisher's chart. This page recommends no congregational key, because no melody range has been measured for it. Sing it through with the person who will lead and move the key only if the phrases strain or disappear in your room.

## Plan the form

The song is short and built to repeat. Decide before rehearsal how many times it comes around and whether the band drops out for one of those passes. Decide what happens at the end too: a held chord into the reading, silence, or a direct move into the next song. Write the plan on every chart and in the lyric software. A prayer song that ends by accident undoes the stillness it created.

If it returns every Sunday of Advent, one option is to keep the arrangement the same each week so there is less for the congregation to relearn.

## Rehearse with your team

Test each of these in your room before trusting it. Start with one instrument and one voice and listen to whether the melody carries on its own. Ask the leader to speak the words at tempo before singing them, so the prayer is phrased like a prayer. If a second voice joins, keep it under the melody rather than above it. Give the lyric operator the exact repeat count in writing, and tell the person lighting the candle which repetition is theirs.

## Recording and source notes

Writer: Sandra McCracken. CCLI 7054135. Composition facts and the E, 6/8 and 58 tempo marking come from Integrity's [song page](https://integrityworship.com/songs/come-light-our-hearts-sandra-mccracken/), checked November 8, 2026; the beat unit for that marking is not stated there. Recording dates and vocal credits come from the two Bandcamp pages linked above. No lyrics are reproduced here; use the publisher's chart under your license. This is a different song from the Taizé chant Veni Lumen Cordium, which some catalogs file under a similar English title. Before Sunday, have your leader read Luke 1:78-79 aloud at rehearsal and decide where the candle sits in the song.

title: O Come, All You Unfaithful
summary_theology: A Christmas invitation addressed to the unfaithful, the weary and the ashamed, grounded in the incarnation and the atonement: Christ was born for people who have not earned the invitation.
practical_worship_leadership: Works as a Christmas call to worship or as the song of assurance after a confession, which is how the publisher classifies it. Pair it with a carol the room already knows; its job is to say who the carols are for.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test, since no audio was analyzed for this page. Try the first verse with one voice and one instrument so the invitation is heard as an invitation. Add parts on the later sections, and test whether a plain ending or a build serves the final line better in your room.
editorial_markdown:
## What "O Come, All You Unfaithful" means

The title turns a familiar carol phrase toward the people who assume Christmas is for someone else. The song invites the unfaithful, the weary, the wounded and the ashamed to come to the manger. It grounds that invitation in why Christ came: to be born, to live and to die for exactly those people. The incarnation and the atonement are held together here, which is rarer in Christmas repertoire than it should be. The baby in the song is the Savior on the cross.

Sovereign Grace Music classifies it under Assurance of Pardon and Call to Worship, and both labels describe what it does in a room. It tells the person who walked in carrying a bad year that the invitation includes them.

## What this song offers your service

Use it as the call to worship on a Christmas Sunday or Christmas Eve, where it says out loud who the service is for before the carols begin. Use it after a time of confession, where it answers the confession with welcome. It also works near the end of a service for the people who still have not sung anything.

Its scope is deliberate. It addresses the congregation more than it addresses God, so a song of direct praise after it is one way to complete the movement. On Christmas Eve, one placement that works is before the candle lighting, where it serves as the welcome into the quieter part of the service.

## Scripture for preparation

These are preparation choices, not the publisher's stated sources. Read Luke 5:31-32, where Jesus says he has come to call sinners rather than the righteous, which is the song's invitation in his own words. Romans 5:6-8 names Christ dying for the ungodly while they were still weak, the ground the song stands on. Matthew 11:28-30, the invitation to the weary and burdened, makes a short reading before the first verse.

## Choose the recording and key

The resource for this page is the version on Sovereign Grace Music's Heaven Has Come, sung by Lisa Clow. The official recorded-key [chart for that version](https://sovereigngracemusic.s3.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/20251112105004/o-come-all-you-unfaithful%E2%80%93hhc%E2%80%93rec-d-chart-1.pdf) lists the key of D, a 6/8 meter and a tempo of 56 counted on the dotted quarter. A separate acoustic recording by David Zimmer is in F. Those are two versions of one composition; do not mix the key of one with the feel of the other when you build your chart.

This page recommends no congregational key, because no melody range has been measured for it. Sing the verses with the person who will lead them and change key only if your room needs it.

## Plan the form

The verses carry the invitation, and on the official chart the bridge carries the Lamb and atonement material. Decide before rehearsal which sections you will sing and whether the bridge stays if you shorten the song. Mark where instruments enter, where they thin out, and how the song ends. No audio was analyzed for this page, so test a plain ending and a build and keep the one that serves the text in your room. Write the plan on every chart and in the lyric software, and tell whoever speaks next how the song ends.

## Rehearse with your team

Test each of these in your room before trusting it. Have the leader sing the first verse with one instrument and listen to whether the words are understood on first hearing by someone who has never heard the song. Add voices on the later sections rather than the first. Check that the 6/8 feel stays relaxed and does not drift into a waltz. Confirm the lyric operator has the section order and that the title is spelled with the comma.

## Recording and source notes

Writers: Bob Kauflin and Lisa Clow. CCLI 7160115. Copyright 2020. Composition facts and the publisher's classification come from the [Sovereign Grace Music song page](https://sovereigngracemusic.com/music/songs/o-come-all-you-unfaithful/), checked November 8, 2026. The D, 6/8 and dotted-quarter 56 values belong to the Heaven Has Come recorded-key chart linked above and to no other version. An official Spanish translation, Oh Ven, Tú Que Eres Infiel, exists as a [separate chart](https://sovereigngracemusic.s3.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/20230821175028/o_come_all_you_unfaithful-spanish.docx-2.pdf); it is the same composition, not a different song. This is a different song from the traditional carol O Come, All Ye Faithful. No lyrics are reproduced here; use the publisher's chart under your license. Before Sunday, have your leader read Luke 5:31-32 aloud and choose the one sentence that introduces the song.

title: Sing We the Song of Emmanuel
summary_theology: A modern carol of adoration that names the child as Emmanuel, God with us, and turns the congregation outward to carry the news, joining Christmas praise to the mission it produces.
practical_worship_leadership: Works as a Christmas opener, as the praise after a nativity reading, or as a sending song at the end of a service. The publisher lists Advent, Epiphany and missions among its themes, so it has a life after December 25.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test, since no audio was analyzed for this page. Decide how the energy grows across the verses and keep the melody singable for a room that is hearing it for the first time. Plan the final chorus so the band and the congregation arrive together rather than the band alone.
editorial_markdown:
## What "Sing We the Song of Emmanuel" means

The song is a call to sing about the child who is God with us, and it keeps widening the circle of who is doing the singing. It begins in adoration at the manger and ends with the congregation carrying the news out. That outward turn is the song's distinctive move. Getty Music lists adoration, Advent, Epiphany and evangelism and missions among its themes, and all four are in the text.

For a congregation, it supplies the praise that the nativity readings ask for and then gives that praise somewhere to go.

## What this song offers your service

Open a Christmas service with it, where its first lines gather the room into singing. Place it after the Luke 2 reading, where the angels' announcement needs a congregational answer. Or close with it, where the outward turn sends the room out. It also fits Epiphany Sunday, when the magi's arrival makes the mission theme the point of the service.

Its limit is tone. It is an announcement song, so it does not do the work of waiting or lament. If your church holds announcement songs until later in Advent, this one waits well; if your church sings carols through the season, it opens a set.

## Scripture for preparation

These are preparation choices, not the writers' stated sources. Read Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:21-23 together, the promise of the virgin's son called Immanuel and Matthew's naming of Jesus as that promise kept; the song's title rests on those verses. Luke 2:10-14, the angels' good news of great joy for all the people, gives you the reading before the first verse and the reason the song ends by sending people out.

## Choose the recording and key

Getty Music identifies the song as performed by Matt Boswell & Matt Papa on its [store page](https://gettymusic.store/collections/sing-we-the-song-of-emmanuel/products/sing-we-the-song-of-emmanuel), and their recording appears on the 2019 album His Mercy Is More. Matt Papa's [song page](https://www.mattpapa.com/songs/sing-we-the-song-of-emmanuel) carries the writers' own notes and resources. No key, tempo or meter for that 2019 recording was verified for this page, so none is listed.

Worship Together lists a separate version titled Sing We the Song of Emmanuel (Gloria) by Keith and Kristyn Getty, Matt Papa and Matt Boswell on its [song page](https://www.worshiptogether.com/songs/sing-we-the-song-of-emmanuel-gloria-keith-and-kristyn-getty-matt-papa-matt-boswell/). That listing gives the key of E, 117 BPM and recommended keys of D, E and F. Those values belong to that Gloria session and should not be copied onto the 2019 recording or onto your chart without checking the version you are using. This page recommends no congregational key, because no melody range has been measured for it.

## Plan the form

Decide which version you are building from, then plan how the energy grows from the first verse to the last. Mark the point where the full band enters and keep the earlier verses lighter so the growth is heard. If you use it as a closer, decide whether the last chorus repeats and who speaks after it. Write the order on every chart and in the lyric software. If your version has a Gloria refrain, keep it in the same place every time so the congregation can anticipate it.

## Rehearse with your team

Test each of these in your room before trusting it. Have the leader sing the first verse alone and ask a listener whether the melody is learnable on one hearing; a carol a room cannot catch quickly is not doing a carol's job. Set the tempo from the version you chose rather than from memory of another. Confirm the drummer and the lyric operator agree on where the last chorus begins. Keep the final line clear, since it is the sentence the room leaves on.

## Recording and source notes

Writers: Matt Boswell, Matt Papa, Keith Getty and Stuart Townend. CCLI 7078042. Copyright 2015. Writer, performer and theme facts come from the [Getty Music store page](https://gettymusic.store/collections/sing-we-the-song-of-emmanuel/products/sing-we-the-song-of-emmanuel) and [Matt Papa's song page](https://www.mattpapa.com/songs/sing-we-the-song-of-emmanuel), checked November 8, 2026. The E, 117 BPM and D, E, F recommendations come from Worship Together's Gloria listing and apply to that version only. This is a different song from Emmanuel (Hallowed Manger Ground), from O Come O Come Emmanuel and from the traditional Gloria. The Getty medley that joins it to O Come O Come Emmanuel is an arrangement, not another composition. No lyrics are reproduced here; use the publisher's chart under your license. Before Sunday, have your leader read Luke 2:10-14 aloud at rehearsal and choose where the song sits in relation to that reading.

title: He Who Is Mighty
summary_theology: A song shaped by Mary's praise in Luke 1 that marvels at the mighty God who did great things by coming low. It holds the humility of the incarnation and the power of the one who came in the same breath.
practical_worship_leadership: Works as the response to a reading of the Magnificat or of Isaiah 9, as a reflective Advent song in the later weeks, or as a quieter Christmas Eve selection before the candle lighting. Keep it with the readings it echoes.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test, since no audio was analyzed for this page. Start with piano or guitar and one voice, let the 6/8 feel breathe rather than march, decide where a second voice enters, and test how the ending resolves before you settle it.
editorial_markdown:
## What "He Who Is Mighty" means

The song takes its shape from Mary's words in Luke 1: the Mighty One has done great things. It marvels that the God who is strong chose to come low, that the one with power arrived as a child, and it keeps those two truths together rather than picking one. The publisher lists Psalm 52:8, Isaiah 9:2-7 and Luke 1:46-49 as its scripture. The song moves across all three: trust in God's steady love, the promised child who carries the government on his shoulders, and the young woman who sang first.

That makes it a praise song with a bowed head, a useful thing to have between the longing songs and the loud ones.

## What this song offers your service

Place it directly after a reading of the Magnificat, on the fourth Sunday of Advent or whenever your church reads Luke 1, where it gives the congregation Mary's response in their own mouths. It also answers an Isaiah 9 reading well. On Christmas Eve it suits the reflective stretch before the candle lighting.

Its scope is adoration and wonder. It does not announce the nativity story itself, so one option is to set it beside a reading or a carol that does and let it be the room's answer.

## Scripture for preparation

The publisher's own references are Psalm 52:8, Isaiah 9:2-7 and Luke 1:46-49. Read Luke 1:46-55 in full at rehearsal so the leader hears the whole of Mary's song and not only the verses the lyric echoes. Isaiah 9:6-7 makes a strong reading before the first verse. Psalm 52:8, the olive tree trusting in God's steadfast love, is a quieter choice for a prayer before the song.

## Choose the recording and key

The resource for this page is the version on Sovereign Grace Music's Prepare Him Room, which credits Rebecca Elliott and Kate DeGraide as vocalists. The official recorded-key [guitar chart](https://sovereigngracemusic.s3.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/20230821181658/he_who_is_mighty-rec_e-guitar.pdf) lists the key of E, a 6/8 meter and a tempo of 51 counted on the dotted quarter. Charts in G circulate widely, and they are alternate-key charts, not evidence that the recording was made in G.

This page recommends no congregational key, because no melody range has been measured for it. Sing it with the person who will lead and move the key only if your room needs it.

## Plan the form

The song is reflective, so plan its dynamics in advance rather than letting them drift. Decide where the second voice joins, whether any section repeats, and how the ending resolves. The recording is one model and your room is another, so test a settled ending and a fuller one in rehearsal. Write the plan on every chart and in the lyric software, and tell whoever reads or prays next how the song ends.

## Rehearse with your team

Test each of these in your room before trusting it. Have the leader sing the first verse over a single instrument and listen for whether the 6/8 feel stays unhurried at the chart's slow tempo. It is easy to let it swing faster than written. If two vocalists lead, as on the recording, rehearse who carries the melody and who sits under it. Confirm the lyric operator knows which reading precedes the song and does not advance the slide until the reader finishes.

## Recording and source notes

Writers: Rebecca Elliott and Kate DeGraide. CCLI 7031870. Copyright 2014. Composition facts, vocalist credits and scripture references come from the [Sovereign Grace Music song page](https://sovereigngracemusic.com/music/songs/he-who-is-mighty/), checked November 8, 2026. The E, 6/8 and dotted-quarter 51 values belong to the Prepare Him Room recorded-key chart linked above and to no other version. An official Spanish version, El Dios Poderoso, translated by Fabrizio Rodulfo, shares this CCLI number on its [song page](https://sovereigngracemusic.com/music/songs/el-dios-poderoso/). It is the same composition, and the English musical values above are not to be assumed for it. This is a different song from He Who Is to Come, from El Poderoso de Israel and from Poderoso Para Salvar. Its Luke 1:49 echo does not make it the same as Great Things. No lyrics are reproduced here; use the publisher's chart under your license. Before Sunday, have your leader read Luke 1:46-55 aloud at rehearsal and choose the sentence that introduces the song.

title: Joy Has Dawned
summary_theology: A narrative modern carol that tells the birth of Christ as the dawn of joy for the world and carries the story through to the cross. The manger and the redemption it began are sung as one event.
practical_worship_leadership: Works as the carol paired with the Luke 2 nativity readings, as a Christmas Day congregational carol, or as a teaching carol where the service wants the whole story in one song. Keep it with the readings; it is written to tell the story.
arrangement_tips: Suggestions to test, since no audio was analyzed for this page. Treat it like a hymn with verses that each carry a scene. Keep a steady tempo across the verses, vary the accompaniment by scene rather than by volume alone, and plan which verses you sing if your slot is short.
editorial_markdown:
## What "Joy Has Dawned" means

The song tells the Christmas story in order and does not stop at the manger. The birth is sung as the moment joy dawned on the world, and the shepherds and the magi arrive in their turn. Then the carol carries the child forward to the cross, where the reason for the birth becomes plain. Stuart Townend has written that it came out of a project working through the Apostles' Creed, with the incarnation as its emphasis. The carol reads like a creed set to music, moving through who he is, what he did and why it matters.

That is what it adds to a Christmas set. It sings the whole arc in one carol, and it lets a congregation say out loud that the baby and the Savior are the same person.

## What this song offers your service

Pair it with the nativity readings on Christmas Eve or Christmas Day. Its early verses follow Luke 2 and its magi verse belongs with Matthew 2. Its later verses go past the nativity readings to the cross, so the carol will outrun a Luke 2 reading on purpose. It also serves a Lessons and Carols service, where its verses can be split across readings, and it has a place at Epiphany, where the magi verse carries the story forward.

Its scope is wide by design, which means it does not sit well as a short response or under a candle lighting. Give it room to tell its story.

## Scripture for preparation

These are preparation choices, not the writers' stated sources. Read Luke 2:1-20 and Matthew 2:1-12 before rehearsal and note which verse of the carol sings which scene. The magi are in Matthew, not Luke, and the cross is in neither nativity reading. John 1:14, the Word made flesh, grounds the first verse. Philippians 2:6-8, the one who emptied himself and became obedient to death on a cross, is where the carol ends up. Reading it after the song is one way to let the last verse land.

## Choose the recording and key

No specific recording was verified for this page. Worship Together's [song page](https://www.worshiptogether.com/songs/joy-has-dawned-keith-and-kristyn-getty/?nav=1) lists the song under Keith & Kristyn Getty. It gives an original key of D sharp, which it also gives as E flat, and a recommended key of E. The Getty hymnal arrangement, available as a [PDF score](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5716a5ea7da24f462d7beeca/t/5fac562bff73a225b2282a01/1748546477935/357_joy_has_dawned_hymnal.pdf), is in F with a tempo of 128 counted on the quarter note. That tempo belongs to that score and should not be read as the tempo of any recording. No meter or vocal range was verified for this page, so none is listed.

This page recommends no congregational key, because no melody range has been measured for it. Sing the verses with the person who will lead and settle the key in your room.

## Plan the form

Decide which verses you will sing. If your slot is short, choose the verses that match the readings you are using rather than cutting from the end, because the final verse is where the carol makes its point. Keep the tempo steady across verses; a narrative carol loses its thread if each verse is a different speed. Mark the accompaniment changes by scene, lighter for the manger and fuller for the angels, and write the order on every chart and in the lyric software.

## Rehearse with your team

Test each of these in your room before trusting it. Have the leader read the verses aloud as a story before singing them, so the phrasing follows the narrative and everyone knows which verses go beyond the readings. Check that the room can keep up with the words; a carol with this much text needs clear diction and clear slides. If you split verses across readings, rehearse the reader and the band together so each verse begins without a gap. Confirm the lyric operator has the final verse order in writing.

## Recording and source notes

Writers: Keith Getty and Stuart Townend. CCLI 4408246. Copyright 2004. The expanded writer's title is Joy Has Dawned Upon the World. Origin and emphasis come from [Stuart Townend's song page](https://www.stuarttownend.co.uk/song/joy-has-dawned/), checked November 8, 2026. Key values come from Worship Together's Keith & Kristyn Getty listing and the hymnal tempo from the Getty score linked above; each belongs to its own source, and neither identifies a specific recording. A Getty medley pairing it with Angels We Have Heard on High exists on [An Irish Christmas](https://gettymusic.store/products/angels_we_have_heard_on_high_an_irish_christmas); it is an arrangement, not a second composition. This is a different song from Joy to the World in both its traditional and Getty and Townend settings, and from Angels We Have Heard on High. No lyrics are reproduced here; use the publisher's chart under your license. Before Sunday, have your leader read Luke 2:1-20 and Matthew 2:1-12 aloud at rehearsal and mark which carol verses answer those readings and which go beyond them.
